1.pericope_label: Afterward he brought me to the gate, even the gate that looketh toward the east: and, behold, the glory of the God of Israel came from the way of the east
debates: Whose glory returns to the house
Why the glory comes from the east
Whether the voice is thunder or speech
outliers: Clarke identifies the appearance with the chariot of cherubim seen at the river Chebar, where Gill identifies it with Christ and Henry with the God in covenant with Israel
Wesley grounds the eastward approach simply in the fact that the glory had departed eastward, while Clarke makes it a general law that knowledge and religion travel from east to west
themes: A splendid house that is still a body without breath
Idols that owe their glory to the goldsmith
Light diffusing westward with the course of the sun
A voice like many waters that is nevertheless articulate

3.pericope_label: And it was according to the appearance of the vision which I saw, even according to the vision that I saw when I came to destroy the city: and the glory of the Lord came into the house
debates: Why the prophet is carried into the inner court
Who speaks out of the house
Who the man standing by is
outliers: Wesley says flatly that the man standing by is Christ, where Ellicott notes the word lacks the article in the Hebrew and takes him for the guide who had been doing the measuring
Clarke turns the lifting by the Spirit into a survey of the whole missionary history of the church, a scale of application the others do not attempt here
themes: A house measured and fitted before its owner moves in
Glory that went out with the sin and returns with the repentance
A man lying on his face until a wind lifts him
A word to be heard as more than the word of man

7.pericope_label: And he said unto me, Son of man, the place of my throne, and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell in the midst of the children of Israel for ever
debates: What the carcases of their kings are
What setting a threshold by God threshold means
Whether the verbs are commands or predictions
outliers: Clarke takes the carcases literally of royal burials near the temple and Wesley of burials in idol temples, while Henry and Ellicott make them the idols themselves, Ellicott arguing that no king is known to have been buried in the Temple area
Ellicott insists that both clauses others read as commands are simple futures, in keeping with the ideal character of the vision, so that the passage predicts the cleansing rather than demanding it
themes: Images called kings and lords that were really dead carcases
Only a wall standing between God and the idols
A door into the church that God never appointed
A dwelling promised for ever where earlier ones passed away

10.pericope_label: Thou son of man, shew the house to the house of Israel, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities: and let them measure the pattern
debates: Who the house is to be shown to
Whether the shame comes before or after the showing
How far the holiness of the mountain extends
outliers: Clarke makes the whole mountain from top to bottom most holy, with no spot appropriated to common use, while Wesley keeps a degree of difference, the circuit holy and the top most holy

Ellicott reads the conditional clause as grammar rather than as a term, holding that the sanctification of the people and the dwelling of God are correlative facts neither of which could stand without the other
themes: A pattern given so that people may measure themselves by it
A congregation blushing at the glory their sins had ruined
More light given to those already made penitent
A mountain with no spot left for common use

13.pericope_label: And these are the measures of the altar after the cubits: The cubit is a cubit and an hand breadth; even the bottom shall be a cubit, and the breadth a cubit
debates: How long the cubit is and how high the altar
What the names Harel and the lion of God mean
Whether the priests went up by steps or a ramp
outliers: Clarke makes the cubit a handbreadth or four inches longer than the Babylonian cubit, while Wesley makes the excess three inches and the whole cubit twenty-one inches

Wesley has the priests climb by steps of about a quarter of a cubit each, where Clarke says the ascent was an inclined plane; Gill and Clarke also differ on whether the fourteen-cubit settle is the top of the altar or the ledge the priests walked on
themes: An altar that looked like a mountain standing in a court
A hearth named for a lion because it devours what is laid on it
Priests on two levels handing the offering upward
An altar built to stay where it was put

18.pericope_label: And he said unto me, Son of man, thus saith the Lord God; These are the ordinances of the altar in the day when they shall make it, to offer burnt offerings thereon, and to sprinkle blood thereon
debates: Who the seed of Zadok are
Whether the prophet himself performs the consecration
Where the bullock of the sin offering is burnt
outliers: Wesley has the bullock burnt in the court of the house and on the altar appointed, while Ellicott argues it must be outside the sanctuary building altogether, in the separate structure described earlier
Ellicott observes that the anointing with oil which opened the consecration of the older altar is here wholly omitted, and explains the silence by the prophet assuming a known ritual
themes: An altar that must be consecrated before it is used
A prophet told to do what he only foretells
A consecration that begins with a confession of sin
A victim carried outside the sanctuary to be burnt

22.pericope_label: And on the second day thou shalt offer a kid of the goats without blemish for a sin offering; and they shall cleanse the altar, as they did cleanse it with the bullock
debates: Why the ritual differs from the older law
Why the burnt offering is not named on the first day
Whether the hand filled is the priests or the altars
outliers: Gill takes the departures from the older ritual as proof that the ceremonial law is changeable and now abolished, while Clarke calls these in general ordinances of the Law and explains the detail by supposing the prophet wrote as if the book of the law had perished
Ellicott declines the emended reading the version follows and keeps the literal text, which fills the hand of the altar rather than of the worshippers
themes: A ceremony that does not match the book it appeals to
Salt thrown rather than sprinkled
A hand filled with the gifts it is to offer
Persons accepted first and then their performances
